stem: w = np.array([0.6, 0.4]); the assets have volatilities of 10% and 20% and a correlation of 0.3. What does np.sqrt(w @ cov @ w) return, expressed as a percentage?

rationale.A: Incorrect. 14.00% is the weighted average of volatilities, which is only correct when the correlation is 1.
rationale.B: Correct. The quadratic form gives a variance of 0.01288 and a volatility of 11.35%.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 10.00% ignores the covariance term, as if the correlation were zero.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 10.70% includes the covariance term only once instead of twice (the off-diagonal appears in two cells of the matrix).

stem: Asset 1 has volatility 15%, asset 2 has volatility 25%, and their correlation is 0.2. The weight in asset 1 of the two-asset minimum-variance portfolio is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 62.50% is inverse-volatility weighting, which ignores correlation and uses volatility rather than variance.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 73.53% is inverse-variance weighting, which is the minimum-variance answer only when the correlation is zero.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 21.43% is the weight in asset 2, not asset 1.

stem: To find the maximum-Sharpe portfolio with scipy.optimize.minimize, the objective function should return:
options: the negative of the portfolio Sharpe ratio
the sum of the weights minus 1
explanation: minimize only minimises. Minimising −SR is the same as maximising SR.

rationale.A: Correct. Minimising the negative Sharpe ratio maximises the Sharpe ratio.
rationale.B: Incorrect. Minimising the Sharpe ratio would find the worst risk-adjusted portfolio.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Minimising variance gives the minimum-variance portfolio, not the tangency portfolio.
rationale.D: Incorrect. That expression belongs in the budget equality constraint, not the objective.

stem: An analyst builds the efficient frontier in a loop with the constraint {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: w @ mu - tgt} and stores the constraints from every iteration, solving them all only after the loop ends. Every frontier point comes out identical. Why?
options: minimize ignores equality constraints when bounds are supplied
w @ mu must be replaced with np.dot(mu, w)
The lambda looks up tgt when it is called, so every stored constraint uses the final target; binding it with lambda w, t=tgt: w @ mu - t fixes this
The covariance matrix must be inverted before each call
explanation: Python closures bind variables late: the lambda reads tgt at call time, not at creation time. A default argument freezes the value for each iteration.

rationale.A: Incorrect. SLSQP handles bounds and equality constraints together.
rationale.B: Incorrect. w @ mu and np.dot(mu, w) give the same number for 1-D arrays.
rationale.C: Correct. Late binding makes every constraint use the last tgt; the default-argument trick captures each value.
rationale.D: Incorrect. The optimiser works with the covariance matrix directly; no inversion is required.
